decks.title: Everyday Spelling Warm-Up
decks.instructions: Listen carefully, type each word, and build confidence with everyday school and home vocabulary.

words.definition: A place where children go to learn.
words.exampleSentence: The children arrived at school early in the morning.
words.hint: It begins with s and ends with l.

words.definition: A piece of ground where flowers or plants grow.
words.exampleSentence: We planted tomatoes in the garden behind the house.
words.hint: It has two syllables and starts with g.

words.definition: An opening in a wall fitted with glass.
words.exampleSentence: Please open the window and let fresh air inside.
words.hint: It begins with w and has the word win at the start.

words.definition: A large cloth used for warmth on a bed.
words.exampleSentence: She covered the baby with a soft blanket.
words.hint: It starts with bl and ends with et.

words.definition: The early part of the day before noon.
words.exampleSentence: We read our storybook every morning.
words.hint: It begins with m and has ing at the end.

words.definition: Very pleasing to look at or hear.
words.exampleSentence: The garden looked beautiful after the rain.
words.hint: It starts with beau and has three syllables.

words.definition: Kind and pleasant to others.
words.exampleSentence: Our new neighbour is friendly and cheerful.
words.hint: It ends with ly and starts with fr.

words.definition: Having great value or meaning.
words.exampleSentence: It is important to listen when the teacher speaks.
words.hint: It begins with im and ends with ant.

decks.title: Nature and Science Spellings
decks.instructions: Practise science-related words that help you talk about the world around you.

words.definition: The invisible mixture of gases around us.
words.exampleSentence: Plants, animals, and people all need air to live.
words.hint: It is a short word with three letters.

words.definition: A living thing that grows in soil or water.
words.exampleSentence: We watered the plant after class.

words.definition: A living thing that can move and breathe.
words.exampleSentence: A goat is an animal that lives on many farms.
words.hint: It begins with a and has three syllables.

words.definition: The condition of the air at a certain time.
words.exampleSentence: The weather is sunny today.

words.definition: To carry people or goods from one place to another.
words.exampleSentence: Buses transport children safely to school.

words.definition: The natural world and surroundings where we live.
words.exampleSentence: We should keep the environment clean.
words.hint: It starts with en and ends with ment.

decks.title: Reading and Writing Spellings
decks.instructions: Practise useful reading and writing words that help learners speak and write with confidence.

words.definition: A group of words that makes complete sense.
words.exampleSentence: Write one sentence about your best friend.
words.hint: It starts with sen and ends with ce.

words.definition: A drawing or image that shows something.
words.exampleSentence: The picture in the book shows a busy market.

words.definition: A person who helps students learn.
words.exampleSentence: Our teacher explained the topic clearly.
words.hint: It begins with tea but is not the drink.

words.definition: A place where books are kept for reading.
words.exampleSentence: We visited the library to borrow a storybook.
words.hint: It starts with li and ends with ry.

words.definition: Something asked in order to get an answer.
words.exampleSentence: The student raised her hand to ask a question.

words.definition: To know the meaning of something clearly.
words.exampleSentence: I understand the lesson better after practice.

decks.title: Academic Vocabulary Challenge
decks.instructions: Strengthen your classroom language with words you meet in reading, science, and social studies.

words.definition: A number that shows part of a whole.
words.exampleSentence: One half is a fraction.
words.hint: It starts with fr and ends with tion.

words.definition: A group of related sentences on one main idea.
words.exampleSentence: Write one paragraph about your favourite season.

words.definition: A scientific test done to learn something.
words.exampleSentence: The class did an experiment with water and ice.
words.hint: It starts with ex and ends with ment.

words.definition: Travel from one place to another.
words.exampleSentence: The family began a long journey by train.

decks.title: Science and Society Spellings
decks.instructions: Build stronger subject vocabulary with words from science, social studies, and mathematics.

words.definition: Something useful that people can use.
words.exampleSentence: Water is an important natural resource.
words.hint: It begins with re and ends with ce.

words.definition: The measure of how hot or cold something is.
words.exampleSentence: The temperature was high in the afternoon.

words.definition: One of the large land areas of the world.
words.exampleSentence: Africa is a continent with many countries.
words.hint: It begins with con and ends with ent.

words.definition: A mathematical process of sharing into equal parts.
words.exampleSentence: We used division to share the oranges equally.

words.definition: A group of people living in the same place.
words.exampleSentence: Everyone in the community helped to clean the park.

words.definition: A substance that helps living things grow and stay healthy.
words.exampleSentence: Plants need nutrients from the soil.
words.hint: It starts with nu and ends with ent.

decks.title: Advanced Word Power
decks.instructions: Practise mature academic words that appear across subjects and formal writing.

words.definition: Detailed examination of something.
words.exampleSentence: Her analysis of the poem was thoughtful and clear.

words.definition: An idea that can be tested.
words.exampleSentence: The student wrote a hypothesis before the experiment.

words.definition: A duty or task that one is expected to do.
words.exampleSentence: Leadership comes with responsibility.

decks.title: Exam and Reasoning Vocabulary
decks.instructions: Practise formal words that appear in secondary school tests, reports, and subject explanations.

words.definition: Careful judgement about the value or quality of something.
words.exampleSentence: The teacher wrote an evaluation of the project.

words.definition: A mathematical statement showing two expressions are equal.
words.exampleSentence: The student solved the equation correctly.

words.definition: A living thing such as a plant, animal, or tiny microbe.
words.exampleSentence: Every organism needs energy to survive.

words.definition: A system of government in which people have the power to choose leaders.
words.exampleSentence: The class learned how democracy gives citizens a voice.

words.definition: An explanation of the meaning of something.
words.exampleSentence: Her interpretation of the poem was thoughtful.

words.definition: Important enough to deserve attention.
words.exampleSentence: There was a significant change in the test results.

cards.back: Air is the invisible mixture of gases all around us. People, animals, and plants need it to live.
We cannot usually see air, but we can feel it when the wind blows or a fan is on.
Air is important because living things need it for breathing and burning.

cards.front: Name one place where air is found.
cards.back: Air is found everywhere around us, including in the classroom, at home, and outdoors.

cards.front: How can moving air help us?
cards.back: Moving air can cool us, dry clothes, and help seeds spread.

cards.front: Give one example of air in action.
cards.back: A balloon fills up because air goes inside it.
A plant is a living thing that grows in soil or water and makes its own food.

cards.front: What do plants need to grow?
cards.back: Plants need air, sunlight, water, and soil or nutrients to grow well.

cards.front: Name one part of a plant.
cards.back: Some parts of a plant are the root, stem, leaf, flower, and fruit.
The root holds the plant in the soil and takes in water and nutrients.
Plants give us food, shade, medicine, and clean air.

cards.front: Give one example of a plant product.
cards.back: Fruit, vegetables, wood, and cotton all come from plants.
A living thing is something that grows, breathes, moves, feeds, and reproduces.
A non-living thing does not grow, breathe, feed, or reproduce.

cards.front: Name two examples of living things.
cards.back: Examples of living things are a dog, a tree, a fish, and a human being.

cards.front: Name two examples of non-living things.
cards.back: Examples of non-living things are a chair, a stone, a book, and a table.
Living things need air, water, food, and a suitable place to live.

cards.front: How can you tell a plant is living?
cards.back: A plant is living because it grows, needs water and air, and can reproduce.
Transportation is the movement of people and goods from one place to another.

cards.front: Name the three main types of transportation.
cards.back: The three main types are land transportation, water transportation, and air transportation.

cards.front: Give one example of land transportation.
cards.back: Examples include bus, car, bicycle, train, and motorcycle.

cards.front: Give one example of water transportation.
cards.back: Examples include canoe, boat, ferry, and ship.
Transportation helps people travel to school, work, hospitals, shops, and other communities.

cards.front: What safety rule should we follow when using transport?
cards.back: We should obey road and transport safety rules, board carefully, and respect drivers and other passengers.
A family is a group of people related by birth, marriage, or care who live together or support one another.

cards.front: Who are members of a family?
cards.back: Family members may include parents, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins.
Family gives love, care, protection, guidance, and support.

cards.front: Name one duty children can do in the family.
cards.back: Children can help with simple chores, respect elders, and keep their things tidy.

cards.front: What is cooperation in the family?
cards.back: Cooperation means family members helping one another and working together peacefully.

cards.front: How can family members show love?
cards.back: They can speak kindly, help each other, share, and care for one another.
A noun is a naming word for a person, place, animal, or thing.
A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun, such as he, she, it, or they.
A verb is an action word or a being word. It tells what someone does or is.
An adjective is a describing word. It tells us more about a noun.
An adverb tells how, when, where, or how often something happens.

cards.front: Why are parts of speech important?
cards.back: They help us understand the job each word is doing so we can read, write, and speak clearly.
A noun is a naming word for a person, place, animal, or thing.
A verb is an action word or a being word.

cards.front: Give one example of a noun.
cards.back: Examples of nouns are teacher, Lagos, goat, apple, and table.

cards.front: Give one example of a verb.
cards.back: Examples of verbs are run, jump, read, sing, is, and are.

cards.front: How do nouns and verbs work together?
cards.back: A noun tells who or what the sentence is about, and a verb tells what the noun is doing or being.

cards.front: Find the noun and verb in 'The girl sings loudly.'
cards.back: The noun is girl and the verb is sings.
Multiplication means adding equal groups again and again.
6 x 1 = 6 because any number multiplied by 1 stays the same.
4 x 0 = 0 because any number multiplied by 0 equals 0.
Multiplication helps us count quickly and solve repeated addition problems.
Addition means putting numbers or groups together to find the total.
Subtraction means taking away from a number to find what is left.
We use addition when we join groups, count totals, or find how many altogether.
We use subtraction when we remove items, compare amounts, or find how many remain.
Evaporation happens when liquid water changes into water vapour because of heat.
Condensation happens when water vapour cools and turns back into tiny droplets.
Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow, hail, or sleet.

cards.front: Why is the water cycle important?
cards.back: It moves water around Earth and helps supply water for plants, animals, and people.
Collection happens when water gathers in rivers, lakes, oceans, and the ground.

cards.front: What gives energy for the water cycle?
cards.back: The Sun provides the heat energy that starts much of the water cycle.
A simple machine is a tool that makes work easier.

cards.front: Name two examples of simple machines.
cards.back: Examples include lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, and screw.
A lever helps lift or move a load more easily.
An inclined plane is a sloping surface that helps move objects up or down with less effort.
They help people do work with less force, less time, or less difficulty.

cards.front: Give one real-life example of a simple machine.
cards.back: A seesaw is a lever, a knife is a wedge, and a staircase acts like an inclined plane.
A simile compares two things using like or as.
A metaphor compares two things by saying one thing is another.
Personification gives human qualities to animals, objects, or ideas.

cards.front: Why do writers use figures of speech?
cards.back: They make writing more vivid, imaginative, and memorable.

cards.front: Give an example of a simile.
cards.back: "As brave as a lion" is a simile.

cards.front: How is a metaphor different from a simile?
cards.back: A simile uses like or as, but a metaphor does not.
A tense shows the time when an action happens.
Present tense shows an action happening now or usually, such as 'She reads every day.'
Past tense shows an action that already happened, such as 'She read yesterday.'
Future tense shows an action that will happen later, such as 'She will read tomorrow.'
Tenses help readers and listeners know when an action happened.

cards.front: Change 'They play football' to past tense.
cards.back: The past-tense sentence is 'They played football.'
A fraction is a number that shows part of a whole.

cards.front: What do the top and bottom numbers in a fraction mean?
cards.back: The top number is the numerator and the bottom number is the denominator.
1/2 means one out of two equal parts.
1/2 is greater than 1/4.

cards.front: How can fractions be seen in daily life?
cards.back: Fractions appear when sharing food, measuring ingredients, or dividing shapes into equal parts.
Equivalent fractions are different fractions that have the same value, such as 1/2 and 2/4.
A natural resource is something found in nature that people use.
Examples are water, soil, air, forests, sunlight, and minerals.
Natural resources provide food, water, shelter, energy, and materials for daily life.
Conservation means using resources wisely and protecting them from waste or damage.

cards.front: How can we protect natural resources?
cards.back: We can avoid waste, plant trees, keep water clean, and use resources carefully.

cards.front: Give one example of misuse of resources.
cards.back: Cutting down too many trees without replacing them is misuse of natural resources.
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use sunlight to make food from carbon dioxide and water.
It takes place mainly in the chloroplasts of green plant cells.
Chlorophyll traps light energy needed for photosynthesis.

cards.front: What are the raw materials of photosynthesis?
cards.back: The raw materials are water and carbon dioxide.

cards.front: What are the products of photosynthesis?
cards.back: The products are glucose and oxygen.

cards.front: Why is photosynthesis important to life?
cards.back: It provides food for plants and releases oxygen needed by most living things.
An acid is a substance that can release hydrogen ions in solution and often has a sour taste.
A base is a substance that can accept hydrogen ions and often feels slippery in solution.
An indicator changes colour to show whether a substance is acidic, basic, or neutral.
Neutralisation happens when an acid reacts with a base to form salt and water.

cards.front: Give one common acid and one common base.
cards.back: Lemon juice contains acid, while soap solution is basic.

cards.front: Why are acids and bases important?
cards.back: They are important in industry, cleaning, digestion, farming, and laboratory work.
Force is a push or pull that can change the motion of an object.
Motion is the change in position of an object over time.
Force can start motion, stop motion, speed up motion, slow it down, or change direction.
Friction is a force that opposes motion when two surfaces rub together.

cards.front: Give one example of force in daily life.
cards.back: Kicking a football, pushing a trolley, or pulling a door all involve force.
Friction helps us walk, hold objects, and stop moving vehicles.
An essay is a piece of writing that explains, describes, argues, or narrates an idea in paragraphs.
The introduction presents the topic and prepares the reader for the main points.
Body paragraphs develop the main ideas with explanation, examples, and supporting details.

cards.front: What is the purpose of the conclusion?
cards.back: The conclusion summarizes the main ideas and leaves the reader with a final thought.

cards.front: Why is planning important in essay writing?
cards.back: Planning helps organize ideas clearly before writing the full essay.

cards.front: Name one quality of a good essay.
cards.back: A good essay is clear, organized, relevant, and supported with examples.
A linear equation is an equation in which the highest power of the variable is 1.

cards.front: What is the goal when solving a linear equation?
cards.back: The goal is to find the value of the variable that makes the equation true.
Subtract 5 from both sides to get x = 7.

cards.front: Why must the same operation be done on both sides?
cards.back: Doing the same operation on both sides keeps the equation balanced.
A variable is a symbol, usually a letter, that stands for an unknown value.

cards.front: How can linear equations be useful?
cards.back: They help solve real-life problems involving unknown quantities, costs, distances, and relationships.
